subject: Need help testing assumptions for a multivariate repeated measures analysis

messages.author: 2227afb3fa9f52c7
messages.subject: Need help testing assumptions for a multivariate repeated measures analysis
parts:
Hi folks,
Does anyone know how to test assumptions for a multivariate repeated measures analysis? I'm working off an example in the PLS205 R lab notes (pg. 11 of the attached R lab 789 document). My experimental design is the same, with 2 fixed factors (in my case: site and nutrient level) and repeated measurements through time (3 summers of data). 

The code for running the analysis is working, but I don't know how to test assumptions and this example doesn't show how to do it. I've found some discussion that seems relevant on this stack exchange thread, but haven't been able to figure out a solution I understand and feel confident in, yet. 

Does anyone know how to test assumptions for this kind of analysis? Or, do you have a resource you'd recommend that explains how to do it? 

As an added layer of complication, I'm missing a few datapoints from the third summer because some plots were destroyed in a winter storm, so there are a few na's in that dataset. But even setting that aside, I don't know how to test the assumptions. 

Any guidance would be soooo appreciated. I'm also attaching my code, in case that's useful.

Thank you,
Megan

messages.author: e16affb65d44d10f
messages.subject: Re: Need help testing assumptions for a multivariate repeated measures analysis
parts:
Hi Megan,

I remember that one of the assumptions is that of sphericity. Have a look at these links, maybe you can find what you are looking for in there.
http://people.stfx.ca/smackenz/courses/honours/Repeated%20Measures%20ANOVA%20-%20Ch.10%20Vincent.pdf
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/15207/understanding-repeated-measure-anova-assumptions-for-correct-interpretation-of-s

Also, if you are working with anova(), you need a balanced dataset (i.e., no NA). However, if you are doing an anova through the linear model command (lm() ), these models can deal with NA.

Hope that helps!
Esther

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: Need help testing assumptions for a multivariate repeated measures analysis
parts: Just a note about NA handling with lm(): the default value for the 'na.action' argument of lm() is 'na.omit' (https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/lm.html). So while lm() will work with a dataset or predictors that contain NA values, actually behind the scenes the function is dropping rows of the dataframe if they contain NAs. Just something to pay attention to because the danger is that you can fit a model, but you may be fitting the model to a slightly different dataset than you think because of the NA handling.

Thank you Esther and Evan for your replies! Your points about sphericity tests and lm() dropping NAs are super helpful.

I'm still uncertain what's the best way to test for normality of residuals and homogeneity of variances in a repeated measures experiment with 3 timepoints and 2 fixed factors (Site and Nutrient Level). 

A few specific questions: 
  1. When testing normality of residuals, is it okay to just bin all the year data together as though it's from one year and look at the residuals that way? 
  2. When testing homogeneity of variances, I've seen people say you can just test the homogeneity of variances for between factors only (and not within-factor). Is this true? Does that mean you can bin all three years of data together as though it's from one year and then look at homogeneity of variances of the between-factors that way? 
  3. Alternatively, I've also seen people say you can test homogeneity of variances separately within each timepoint. Is this true? In that case, I would run 3 separate homogeneity of variance tests, one for each year. Not sure if that's an acceptable approach, either.
If anyone knows the answers to any of these questions, I'd really appreciate a point in the right direction.

Thanks again,
Megan

messages.author: 73c3477df3617a0f
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Re: Need help testing assumptions for a multivariate repeated measures analysis
parts:
Hi Megan,

I am going to take a stab at helping out but any corrections from persons with a deeper understanding are welcome.

I think you should always be using the residuals from the full model, so that you are looking at the error between your model prediction and your data, accounting for time point, site, and nutrient level effects. When you do this, it makes sense to consider the normality of the residuals from the full model all together (e.g. using a QQ plot to visualize), but this isn't the same as binning across years 'as though it's from one year'. If you for example calculated residuals from a partial model that didn't account for year effects, and pooled across years to plot, you wouldn't necessarily expect the residuals to look normal because if there is a strong year effect, the residuals would separate out by year, e.g. under-prediction of growth for data points from a 'good' year and over-prediction of growth for data points from a 'bad' year, causing the pooled residuals to have multiple modes (clumps).

I think what you are assuming with 'homogeneity of variances' in a multivariate repeated measures analysis is that the size of the errors (variance of data around the full model prediction) doesn't depend on the model's prediction (fitted value) or any of your predictor values ... so as a first step maybe you could just do a scatter plot of your residuals vs. model prediction and also residuals vs. time point, residuals vs. nutrient level etc. and check that the size of the residuals from your full fitted model doesn't depend on any of your plotted x-values. I am not sure I understand your questions 2) and 3) but I agree with you that it doesn't seem right to pool across a variable as if it doesn't exist nor run 3 separate tests, one for each year. But I *think* if you account for year and site in your model, and use residuals from the full model, you can pool these residuals across years and sites when looking for homogeneous variance across different values of your nutrient variable.

Here is a blog I found that has some rather extreme 'good fit' and 'bad fit' examples with R code (unfortunately with just a basic one variable example): https://biologyforfun.wordpress.com/2014/04/16/checking-glm-model-assumptions-in-r/

I have only seen worked examples of this in a Bayesian context of generalized mixed linear models, but because your storm data is likely 'missing at random' I imagine there is a good way to model your missing points so that you can use all of your data.

I hope this helps!
Cheers,
Erin
